training-and-optimisation.text: A model definition is only a promise. Turning it into something useful means three separate jobs, and they fail in different ways. Optimisation is the machinery that walks a set of numbers toward a lower error. Feature preparation is the work of shaping raw columns into something that machinery can actually move through. And tuning is the outer search over the knobs you chose by hand rather than learned from data. This section splits along those lines because a model that trains badly is usually broken in exactly one of those three places, and the fix is different in each.
training-and-optimisation.deep_text:
The order here is deliberate. Gradient descent comes first because it is the engine underneath most of what follows: it explains what "training" physically does, why it can stall, and why the shape of your data matters to it. Once you understand that training is a repeated small step downhill on an error surface, the second part stops being a list of chores and starts being obvious. Rescaling columns, encoding categories as numbers, filling gaps, dropping useless inputs, and compressing correlated columns are all ways of reshaping that error surface so descent has an easier time and the model has less noise to fit. Feature preparation is optimisation-aware data work, not hygiene for its own sake.

Hyperparameter tuning sits last because it is the outer loop wrapped around the other two. Learning rate, regularisation strength, tree depth, the number of components you kept — none of these are learned by the descent procedure. They are chosen, and choosing them well means running training many times and comparing honestly. That honesty requirement is why validation strategy lives in this part rather than being assumed.

Read them in order the first time. In practice you will cycle: tuning reveals that a feature is scaled wrong, fixing the scaling changes which learning rate works, and the search restarts. What stays constant is the diagnostic habit — when a model underperforms, ask three questions in order. Did the optimiser fail to converge, so the loss never actually got low? Did the features carry no usable signal, so there was nothing to converge to? Or were the settings simply never searched, so a better version of the same model was always available and you never looked? Those three questions map onto the three parts of this section, and answering them in that order saves you from tuning a model whose inputs were broken all along.

gradient-descent.text: Almost every model that learns from data does it by the same trick: measure how wrong you are, work out which direction makes that wrongness smaller, take a small step that way, repeat. That is gradient descent, and it is a general optimisation procedure rather than anything specific to one model family. It breaks into a few questions you have to answer separately. What does the gradient actually tell you? How much data do you look at per step? How big is a step? Can you make steps smarter using history? And what happens when the landscape stops cooperating?
gradient-descent.deep_text:
Start with the gradient itself, because everything else is a modification of it. The gradient is a vector of partial derivatives that points uphill on the loss surface, and descent is simply the decision to go the other way. Getting that geometry straight makes the rest legible.

Next comes the question of how much data each step is computed from. Using the whole training set gives a precise direction but an expensive step; using one example gives a cheap noisy step; the middle ground is what nearly everyone actually runs. This is a compute-versus-noise trade, and it interacts with everything downstream.

Step size is the third question and the one most people get wrong first. Too large and the parameters bounce or diverge; too small and training takes forever and stalls in shallow regions. Convergence behaviour — what the loss curve looks like over time — is the main diagnostic signal you get, so learning to read it is worth more than memorising formulas.

The fourth part improves on plain steps by remembering past ones. Momentum-style methods build up velocity in consistent directions; adaptive methods give each parameter its own effective step size based on how large its gradients have been. These are general-purpose optimisers, usable on any differentiable objective.

Finally, the landscape itself. Not every place the gradient vanishes is a good answer, and the practical failure modes differ from the ones intuition suggests. That part explains why training sometimes flatlines with a loss that has not actually finished falling.

the-gradient-as-direction-of-steepest-as.text: The gradient of a loss function is just a list of slopes, one per parameter, each answering "if I nudge this number up slightly, how much does the error change?" Stack those slopes into a vector and you get the single direction in parameter space along which the error rises fastest. That is why it is called the direction of steepest ascent. Training wants error to fall, so you step along the negative gradient instead. Everything about optimisation follows from this one fact: you have a local compass, it points uphill, and you walk backwards along it.
the-gradient-as-direction-of-steepest-as.deep_text:
Take a loss with two parameters, w and b, and imagine it as a bowl-shaped surface where height is the error. Suppose at your current point the partial derivative with respect to w is 6 and with respect to b is -2. The gradient is the vector (6, -2). That says error climbs fastest if you move w up and b down in a 3-to-1 ratio. Descent flips the sign: you move w down and b up. With a step size of 0.01 you would update w by -0.06 and b by +0.02. Do that repeatedly and you spiral into the bottom of the bowl.

Why steepest, and not just some downhill direction? Because the change in loss for a small step in direction d is approximately the dot product of the gradient with d, and a dot product is maximised when d points the same way as the gradient. Any other downhill direction still reduces loss, just less per unit of distance travelled. This also explains why the magnitude carries information: a large gradient means the surface is steep and you are far from flat ground, a near-zero gradient means the surface is locally flat.

The common misconception is that the gradient points toward the minimum. It does not. It points along the steepest local slope, which is a statement about the ground under your feet and nothing more. On a long narrow valley, the steepest direction is mostly across the valley walls, not along the floor toward the low point — so naive descent zigzags between the walls while creeping slowly forward. The gradient is a local compass with no map.

A second, subtler point: the gradient is defined per parameter, in that parameter's own units. If one input feature ranges over thousands and another over fractions, their corresponding weights get gradients of wildly different magnitude, and a single shared step size cannot serve both well. That is the mathematical reason feature scaling helps optimisation rather than just being tidy.

The decision rule is simple. Gradient descent is available whenever your loss is differentiable with respect to the parameters. When it is not — decision-tree splits, discrete structure searches — you need a different family of methods entirely, and no amount of clever stepping recovers a gradient that does not exist.

interview.question: Why do we move along the negative gradient rather than picking any direction that lowers the loss?
interview.answer: Any descent direction reduces loss, but the negative gradient reduces it fastest per unit of distance moved, because the first-order change in loss is the dot product of the gradient with your step direction, and that is extremised when the direction aligns with the gradient. So it is the greedy local optimum for step efficiency. It is not necessarily the fastest route overall, which is precisely why momentum and second-order corrections exist.

interview.question: A colleague says the gradient points toward the minimum. How would you correct that?
interview.answer: The gradient is purely local — it describes the slope at your current point and knows nothing about where the minimum sits. In an elongated valley the steepest direction points across the valley rather than down its length, so following it produces zigzagging that converges slowly. Curvature information, which the gradient does not carry, is what would actually point you at the minimum.

interview.question: When would you reach for something other than gradient-based optimisation?
interview.answer: When the objective is not differentiable with respect to the parameters you are searching over. Choosing tree splits, selecting a subset of features, or tuning discrete settings all fall in that category, and there is no gradient to follow. Those cases call for combinatorial search, greedy heuristics, or derivative-free methods instead.

batch-stochastic-and-mini-batch-descent.text: The gradient you want is the average over your entire training set, but computing it that way means touching every row before you move a single millimetre. Batch descent does exactly that: exact direction, expensive step. Stochastic descent goes to the other extreme and estimates the gradient from one example, which is fast and very noisy. Mini-batch descent sits in between, averaging over a few dozen to a few hundred examples, and is what almost everyone actually runs. The choice is really about how many steps you can afford per pass over your data.
batch-stochastic-and-mini-batch-descent.deep_text:
Put numbers on it. Say you have 100,000 training rows. Batch descent computes 100,000 gradient contributions, averages them, and takes one parameter update. After a full pass through the data you have moved once. Stochastic descent updates after every single row, so the same pass yields 100,000 updates — each one pointing in a direction that is roughly right but badly contaminated by whatever quirks that particular row has. Mini-batch descent with a batch of 128 gives you about 780 updates per pass, each computed from an average that has cancelled out most of the per-row noise. In wall-clock terms mini-batch usually wins twice over, because averaging 128 examples is a single matrix operation that vectorised hardware handles nearly as fast as one example.

The noise is not purely a cost. A noisy gradient estimate jitters the parameters, and that jitter can shake the optimiser out of shallow bad regions that an exact gradient would sit down in and never leave. This is why pure batch descent is rarely preferred even when you can afford it. The flip side is that the loss curve for mini-batch training is bumpy — it goes down on average but individual steps can increase the loss, and that is normal rather than a bug.

The common misconception is that stochastic descent means picking a random example each time in a literal sense. In practice you shuffle the dataset once per epoch and walk through it in order, which guarantees every example contributes exactly once per pass. Forgetting to shuffle is a real bug: if your data arrived sorted by label, consecutive mini-batches contain only one class, and the parameters swing back and forth chasing whichever class they just saw.

Batch size also interacts with step size. Larger batches give lower-variance gradients, which tolerate and often require larger steps to make comparable progress; shrink the batch and you generally need to shrink the step too, or the noise amplifies into instability.

The decision rule: default to mini-batch, and size the batch by what fits comfortably in memory while keeping your hardware busy. Reach for full-batch only when the dataset is genuinely small or when you need a deterministic, reproducible trajectory — for instance while debugging whether an optimisation problem converges at all. Pure single-example updates are worth it mainly in streaming settings where examples arrive one at a time and you cannot buffer them.

interview.question: Why is mini-batch the default rather than full-batch descent, even when the dataset fits in memory?
interview.answer: Because progress per unit of compute is much better. Full-batch spends an entire pass over the data to make one update, while mini-batch makes hundreds, each from a gradient estimate that is noisy but close enough to be useful. The residual noise is also mildly helpful, since it prevents the optimiser from settling into shallow regions that an exact gradient would not escape.

interview.question: Your training loss is jagged rather than smoothly decreasing. Is that a problem?
interview.answer: Usually not, if the trend is downward — each mini-batch is a different sample, so the loss on each is a different number and small increases are expected. It becomes a problem when the jaggedness grows over time or the trend stops falling, which points to a step size that is too large for the batch size. The fix is to plot a running average and judge the trend, not individual steps.

interview.question: If you doubled your batch size, what else would you reconsider?
interview.answer: The learning rate, primarily. A larger batch gives a lower-variance gradient, so you can afford a bigger step, and keeping the old step size often means slower progress per pass through the data. You would also expect fewer updates per epoch, so any schedule defined in terms of step counts needs rescaling too.

learning-rate-and-convergence-behaviour.text: The gradient tells you which way to go. The learning rate decides how far you commit. Set it too high and the parameters overshoot the bottom, land further up the other side, and the loss climbs or oscillates instead of settling. Set it too low and you crawl, burning compute while the loss barely moves. There is no universally correct value, because the right step depends on the curvature of your loss surface and the scale of your features. Most of the time, the shape of the loss curve tells you which mistake you made.
learning-rate-and-convergence-behaviour.deep_text:
A concrete picture helps. Suppose the loss is a simple parabola whose minimum sits at w equals 5, and you start at w equals 0. With a small learning rate you might move to 0.5, then 0.95, then 1.35 — converging, but slowly enough that a few hundred steps go by before you arrive. With a well-chosen rate you get 3, then 4.5, then 4.9. With a rate that is too large you go from 0 to 9, then back to -4, then out to 18: each step overcorrects harder than the last and the loss diverges. The same three regimes appear on real problems, just in many dimensions at once.

Reading the curve is the practical skill. A loss that drops fast and then flattens at a reasonable value converged. A loss that drops for a while then flattens high has usually stalled — the rate is too small to escape a shallow region, or you have hit a genuinely flat part of the surface. A loss that oscillates with growing amplitude, or that turns into NaN, is unambiguously too large a rate. A loss that decreases in a straight line and has clearly not levelled off just needs more steps.

The common misconception is that a fixed rate that works at the start will keep working. Early in training, gradients are large and you want big steps to cover ground; near the minimum, you want small steps or you rattle around the bottom without settling. That is why schedules exist — decaying the rate over time, or warming it up from a small value before decaying — and why a constant rate often plateaus at a loss slightly worse than the same run with decay.

Feature scale matters here more than people expect. If one feature ranges over thousands and another over fractions, the loss surface becomes a long narrow valley, and the largest rate that is stable along the steep direction is far too small to make progress along the shallow one. No single scalar rate serves both, which is why rescaling inputs often fixes a training problem that looked like an optimiser problem.

The decision rule for finding a value: search on a logarithmic scale, not a linear one. Try values separated by factors of three or ten, run each briefly, and pick the largest one whose loss still falls smoothly. Then, if you care about the last fraction of performance, add decay.

interview.question: Training loss goes to NaN after a few hundred steps. What is your first hypothesis?
interview.answer: The learning rate is too high, so parameters overshoot, gradients grow in response, and the process diverges numerically within a few updates. I would rerun with the rate cut by an order of magnitude and confirm the loss falls smoothly. If it still diverges, I would look for unscaled input features or an exploding term in the loss itself.

interview.question: Why search learning rates logarithmically rather than in even increments?
interview.answer: Because the effect is multiplicative, not additive — the difference between 0.001 and 0.01 is enormous, while the difference between 0.01 and 0.011 is invisible. A linear grid wastes nearly all its evaluations in one narrow band and misses whole regimes. Log spacing covers the range of magnitudes where the behaviour actually changes.

interview.question: When would a decaying schedule beat a well-tuned constant rate?
interview.answer: When you need the final fraction of accuracy. A constant rate large enough to make good early progress is too large to settle precisely at the end, so the loss plateaus while bouncing around the minimum. Decaying lets you keep the fast early phase and then tighten up, which typically buys a slightly lower final loss for no extra compute.

momentum-rmsprop-and-adam.text: Plain descent treats every step as if it had no history and every parameter as if it deserved the same step size. Both assumptions can be improved. Momentum accumulates a running velocity, so consistent directions build speed and directions that keep reversing cancel out. RMSProp keeps a running estimate of how large each parameter's gradients have been and shrinks the step for the noisy ones, giving every parameter its own effective rate. Adam combines the two. These are general-purpose optimisers for any differentiable objective, not tools tied to one model type.
momentum-rmsprop-and-adam.deep_text:
Momentum first. Instead of stepping along the current gradient, you maintain a velocity vector: at each iteration, decay the old velocity by a factor like 0.9 and add the current gradient, then step along that velocity. In a long narrow valley where the gradient alternately points left and right across the walls, those contributions largely cancel, while the small consistent component pointing down the valley floor accumulates. Concretely, if the down-valley gradient is 0.1 every step and the decay is 0.9, the velocity approaches 0.1 divided by 0.1, or 1.0 — a tenfold effective speedup along that axis, while the oscillating component stays small. That is the whole mechanism.

RMSProp attacks a different problem. It keeps an exponentially decaying average of the squared gradient for each parameter and divides that parameter's step by the square root of that average. A parameter whose gradients have been consistently large gets a small divisor-adjusted step; one whose gradients have been tiny gets a relatively larger one. The result is per-parameter normalisation, which matters when different parameters live on wildly different scales — a sparse feature that fires in one row per thousand would otherwise almost never move.

Adam runs both bookkeeping tracks at once: a decaying average of the gradient itself, which is the momentum term, and a decaying average of the squared gradient, which is the RMSProp term. It divides one by the square root of the other. It also applies a bias correction in the early steps, because both averages start at zero and would otherwise be biased toward zero when only a few observations have accumulated. That correction is why Adam behaves sensibly from step one rather than needing a warm-up.

The common misconception is that Adam removes the need to choose a learning rate. It does not. Adam has its own base rate that scales all its steps, and it is still the single most important thing to tune; what Adam removes is the need for that one rate to be simultaneously correct for parameters on very different scales. A related misconception is that the adaptive methods always win. On well-conditioned problems, momentum with a tuned rate and a decay schedule frequently matches or beats them, and sometimes generalises slightly better.

The decision rule: start with Adam when you want something that works without much fiddling, especially on sparse or badly scaled features. Prefer momentum with a schedule when you have the budget to tune properly and want the last increment of quality. If either one diverges, the base rate is still the first knob to touch.

interview.question: What problem does momentum actually solve that a larger learning rate does not?
interview.answer: It handles anisotropy — surfaces that are steep in one direction and shallow in another. Raising the learning rate to speed up the shallow direction destabilises the steep one, whereas momentum cancels the oscillating steep-direction contributions while accumulating the consistent shallow-direction one. It effectively decouples progress along different axes without a single rate having to serve both.

interview.question: Why does Adam need bias correction, and what would happen without it?
interview.answer: Both of its running averages are initialised at zero, so after a handful of steps they are pulled toward zero and underestimate the true magnitudes. Without correction the ratio of the two estimates is skewed and the early steps come out badly sized — typically far too small, then jumping as the averages fill in. The correction divides out the known initialisation bias so the estimates are unbiased from the first step.

interview.question: You are told Adam means you no longer have to tune the learning rate. Do you agree?
interview.answer: No. Adam adapts the relative step size across parameters, but its global base rate still sets the overall scale and is still the highest-impact hyperparameter. What it genuinely buys you is robustness when features or gradients differ by orders of magnitude, where one hand-tuned scalar rate could not work for every parameter at once.

local-minima-saddle-points-and-plateaus.text: Descent stops when the gradient vanishes, but a zero gradient is not proof you found the best answer. It could be a local minimum, a genuine bowl that just is not the deepest one. It could be a saddle point, which curves down in some directions and up in others, so it is a minimum only from certain angles. Or it could be a plateau, a region so flat that gradients are nearly zero and steps barely move anything. Each of these makes training stall, and they call for different responses.
local-minima-saddle-points-and-plateaus.deep_text:
Think about a loss surface over two parameters shaped like a horse saddle. Sit at the centre: move forward or back and the loss rises, move left or right and it falls. The gradient at that exact point is zero, so plain descent sees no reason to move, yet you are nowhere near a minimum. In high dimensions this situation is much more common than a true local minimum, because for a critical point to be a local minimum the surface must curve upward in every single direction at once, and with thousands of parameters the odds of that are poor. The practical consequence is that a stalled optimiser is more often stuck at or near a saddle than trapped in a bad bowl.

Plateaus are a different failure. Consider a loss built from a squashing function whose output saturates: once a parameter drives that function deep into its flat tail, the derivative there is close to zero, so the gradient signal reaching the parameter is close to zero, and the parameter barely updates no matter how wrong it is. The loss curve goes flat while the model is still visibly bad. That is not a critical point — it is a region where the surface is nearly level, and escaping it requires either enough noise to drift out or an optimiser that inflates small consistent gradients.

The common misconception is that local minima are the main obstacle. They dominate the folklore, but on most real problems the observed stalls come from saddles and flat regions, and many local minima that do exist reach loss values close enough to the best that the difference does not matter for prediction quality. Chasing the global minimum is usually the wrong goal; getting the loss low enough that held-out performance stops improving is the real one.

What helps, concretely: gradient noise from mini-batching perturbs the parameters enough to drift off a saddle rather than balancing on it. Momentum carries you through flat regions using accumulated speed from before you entered them. Per-parameter adaptive scaling rescues parameters whose gradients are small but consistent. Restarting from a different random initialisation and comparing final losses is a cheap empirical check on whether you landed somewhere unusually bad.

The decision rule: when the loss flattens high, first confirm the learning rate has not simply decayed to nothing and the features are scaled, since both mimic a plateau. Only then treat it as a landscape problem, and reach for noise, momentum, or a different starting point.

interview.question: Why are saddle points a bigger practical concern than local minima in high-dimensional problems?
interview.answer: A local minimum requires the surface to curve upward along every direction simultaneously, and with many parameters that is a demanding coincidence. Saddle points only require a mix of upward and downward curvature, which is far more likely, so most critical points encountered are saddles. Stochastic noise and momentum help escape them, which is part of why plain full-batch descent stalls more visibly.

interview.question: Training loss has been flat for a long stretch. How do you tell a plateau from convergence?
interview.answer: Compare the flat value to what the problem should achieve and check whether validation performance is also flat — converging at a good loss looks different from stalling at a bad one. I would also check the gradient magnitudes and the current effective learning rate, since a decayed rate produces the same flat curve for a completely different reason. Restarting from another initialisation and seeing a lower plateau is strong evidence you were stuck.

interview.question: Would you invest effort in reaching the global minimum of a training loss?
interview.answer: Generally no. The training loss is a proxy, and driving it to its absolute floor typically means fitting noise, so held-out performance stops improving or degrades before you get there. Effort is better spent making sure the optimiser is not stalling somewhere clearly bad, then judging on validation results rather than on the training objective.

feature-engineering-and-preparation.text: Raw data rarely arrives in a form a model can use. Columns come in wildly different units, some hold text categories rather than numbers, some have gaps, many carry no signal at all, and several say the same thing as each other. Each of those is a distinct problem with a distinct family of fixes: rescale, encode, impute, select, or compress. This part works through them in that order, because they compose — you encode before you can scale, and you scale before compression means anything. Getting this right often moves results more than swapping the model does.
feature-engineering-and-preparation.deep_text:
The sequencing here reflects a real pipeline. Numeric scale comes first conceptually because it is the constraint that most directly affects optimisation and any method that measures distances: features on incomparable ranges distort both. Once you understand why scale matters, encoding follows naturally, since turning categories into numbers is really the question of what numeric structure you are willing to assert about values that have none intrinsically — and the encoding you pick determines what scaling then has to handle.

Missing values sit next because they are a decision, not a cleanup step. Every choice you make about a gap — drop the row, fill it with a summary statistic, model it, or flag it — encodes an assumption about why the value is absent, and that assumption propagates into every downstream number.

The last two parts both reduce how many columns reach the model, but along different axes. Selection keeps a subset of the original columns and throws the rest away, which preserves interpretability because every surviving column still means what it always meant. Compression builds new columns as combinations of the old ones, trading that interpretability for the ability to capture redundancy spread across many correlated inputs at once. Understanding that difference is what tells you which to reach for.

One discipline runs through all five: every transformation must be fitted on training data only and then applied unchanged to validation and test data. A scaler that saw the test set's range, or an imputer that averaged over all rows, has leaked information and will make your evaluation optimistic. In practice this is the single most common way a strong offline result fails to reproduce in production.

normalisation-and-standardisation.text: Features arrive on wildly different scales — annual income in the tens of thousands next to age in the tens next to a ratio between zero and one. Any method that adds weighted inputs or measures distances treats those magnitudes as meaningful, so the large-numbered column dominates purely because of its units. Rescaling fixes that. Min-max normalisation squeezes each column into a fixed range like zero to one. Standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so each column has mean zero and unit spread. Both put columns on comparable footing, in different ways.
normalisation-and-standardisation.deep_text:
Take income ranging from 20,000 to 200,000 and age ranging from 18 to 80. Min-max normalisation maps a 50,000 income to (50000 minus 20000) divided by (200000 minus 20000), which is about 0.17, and a 40-year-old to (40 minus 18) divided by 62, about 0.35. Standardisation instead uses the column statistics: if income has mean 70,000 and standard deviation 40,000, that same 50,000 becomes (50000 minus 70000) divided by 40000, which is -0.5, meaning half a standard deviation below average. Standardised values are unbounded and centred; normalised values are bounded and not centred.

Why this matters for optimisation: unscaled features make the loss surface a long narrow valley, since a weight attached to a feature with huge values produces huge gradients while a weight on a small-valued feature barely moves. A single step size cannot serve both, so training either diverges along one axis or crawls along the other. Rescaling rounds out that valley. It matters just as much for anything computing distances, where income differences of thousands would swamp age differences of decades entirely.

The common misconception is that scaling is always necessary. It is not. Tree-based models split on thresholds within a single column at a time, and a monotone rescaling of a column leaves every possible split ordering identical, so the fitted tree is unchanged. Scaling those models is harmless but pointless. The methods that need it are the ones combining features into a weighted sum, computing distances, or applying penalties that assume comparable coefficient magnitudes.

The second misconception is more damaging: fitting the scaler on the full dataset. The mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum must come from training rows only. Computing them across train and test lets test-set information into the transform, and your held-out score stops being held out.

The decision rule: standardise by default, because it is not thrown off by a single extreme value the way a min-max range is — one outlier at ten times the normal maximum compresses every other row into a thin band near zero. Use min-max when you genuinely need bounded output, and reach for a robust variant based on the median and interquartile range when the column has heavy tails you cannot remove.

interview.question: Why does a tree-based model not need feature scaling while a distance-based one does?
interview.answer: Trees split one feature at a time by comparing values to a threshold, and any monotone rescaling preserves the ordering within that column, so the same split points are available and the fitted tree is identical. Distance-based methods sum contributions across features, so a column measured in thousands contributes far more to the distance than one measured in single digits. There the units, not the information, decide the outcome.

interview.question: When would you choose min-max over standardisation?
interview.answer: When downstream you need values in a guaranteed bounded range — an input constrained to zero-to-one, or a display where interpretability of the bounds matters. The trade-off is fragility: min-max depends on the extremes, so one outlier compresses everything else, and unseen data can fall outside the fitted range. Standardisation degrades more gracefully under both conditions.

interview.question: Where in a cross-validation loop should the scaler be fitted?
interview.answer: Inside each fold, on that fold's training portion only, then applied to its validation portion. Fitting once on the whole dataset leaks the validation rows' statistics into the transform and produces optimistic scores. Wrapping the scaler and model in a single pipeline object is the usual way to make that correct by construction rather than by discipline.

encoding-categorical-variables.text: Models consume numbers, but plenty of real columns hold labels — country, product category, device type. You have to turn those into numbers without accidentally asserting things that are not true. Assigning integers arbitrarily claims an ordering and a spacing that does not exist. One-hot encoding avoids that by giving each category its own binary column, at the cost of width. Ordinal encoding is correct when a genuine order exists, like small, medium, large. Target-based encodings compress high-cardinality columns into one number, but risk leaking the label if done carelessly.
encoding-categorical-variables.deep_text:
Suppose a colour column takes values red, green, and blue. Map them to 1, 2, 3 and feed that to a linear model and you have told it that green sits between red and blue, and that the gap from red to green equals the gap from green to blue. Neither is true, and the model will happily fit a coefficient based on that fiction. One-hot encoding replaces the column with three binary columns — is_red, is_green, is_blue — so each category gets its own independent coefficient and no ordering is implied. For a linear model with an intercept you typically drop one of the three, since the third is fully determined by the other two and keeping all three makes the coefficients non-identifiable.

One-hot breaks down on cardinality. A postcode column with 20,000 distinct values becomes 20,000 columns, most of them almost entirely zero, and any single category might appear in only a handful of training rows. Target encoding is the usual answer: replace each category with a summary of the label for rows in that category — for instance, the average conversion rate among users from that postcode. A postcode with 40 training rows and 12 conversions becomes 0.30.

That is also where the biggest trap lives. If you compute that average using the row you are about to train on, the encoded value contains that row's own label, and the model learns to read the answer off the feature. Training accuracy looks excellent and test performance collapses. The correction is to compute the encoding out-of-fold — for each row, use only the other folds' labels — and to smooth rare categories toward the overall mean, so a postcode with two rows does not get an extreme value from pure noise.

The common misconception is that one-hot is always the safe default. It is safe about ordering but not about width: it can multiply your feature count enormously, slow training, and dilute the signal of rare categories. Tree models in particular struggle with very wide sparse one-hot encodings, because each binary column can only produce one weak split.

The decision rule: use ordinal encoding only when there is a real order and the spacing is defensible. Use one-hot for low cardinality, roughly up to a few dozen levels. Use out-of-fold target encoding above that. And whatever you choose, decide up front what happens to a category that appears at prediction time but never appeared in training — an explicit unknown bucket is the usual answer.

interview.question: Why is assigning arbitrary integers to categories a problem for a linear model but less so for a tree?
interview.answer: A linear model multiplies the encoded value by a single coefficient, so it necessarily assumes the categories are ordered and evenly spaced, which arbitrary integers make false. A tree can carve the integer range into arbitrary intervals with successive splits, so it can partially recover groupings that the numbering scrambled. It still wastes depth doing so, and the recovery is imperfect for many categories.

interview.question: How does target encoding leak, and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: If a category's encoded value is computed from all training labels including the row being encoded, that row's own label bleeds into its feature and the model learns a shortcut that does not exist at prediction time. You prevent it by computing the encoding out-of-fold, so each row's value uses only labels from other folds, and by smoothing rare categories toward the global mean. Without both, training scores look strong and held-out performance falls apart.

interview.question: A category appears in production that was never in your training data. What did you plan for?
interview.answer: An explicit unknown bucket in the encoder, so unseen values map to a defined representation rather than crashing or silently becoming zeros in every one-hot column. For target encoding, the unknown case should fall back to the global mean. I would also monitor the rate of unknown categories over time, since a rising rate usually signals upstream data drift rather than a genuinely new long tail.

handling-missing-values.text: Real datasets have gaps, and how you fill them is a modelling decision rather than housekeeping. Dropping rows is simple but throws away data and biases the result if the missingness is not random. Filling with the column mean or median keeps every row but shrinks the column's variance and pretends you know something you do not. Predicting the missing value from the other columns is more faithful and more work. And often the fact that a value is missing is itself informative, which argues for recording it as an explicit flag alongside whatever you fill in.
handling-missing-values.deep_text:
Consider a survey where income is missing for 15 percent of respondents. Drop those rows and you lose 15 percent of your data, but worse, if high earners are the ones declining to answer, the surviving rows are systematically poorer and every model you fit is biased toward that skew. Fill with the column median — say 52,000 — and you now have a spike of identical values at 52,000 that did not exist in reality. That spike compresses the column's apparent variance, weakens its measured correlation with the target, and makes the model underrate a feature that may actually matter.

Adding an indicator column fixes part of this. Alongside the imputed income you add income_was_missing as a zero-or-one flag. If declining to answer correlates with the outcome, the model can now use that fact directly, and the imputed value stops having to carry two jobs at once. This is cheap and frequently the highest-value move available.

Iterative imputation goes further: treat the column with gaps as a target, fit a model on the rows where it is present using the other columns as inputs, and predict the missing entries. For income, education and postcode might predict it reasonably well. This preserves relationships between columns that a constant fill destroys, at the cost of a fitted model per column and a real risk of overconfidence — the imputed values will look cleaner and more predictable than genuine observations.

The common misconception is that the mean is a neutral default. It is not; it is an assertion that the missing entries look like the average of the observed ones. That is only true when values are missing completely at random, which is rare. A sensor that fails under high load produces gaps precisely where the readings would have been extreme, and mean-filling there erases exactly the signal you wanted.

One practical rule that catches people: fit the imputer on training data only. Computing a median across the full dataset before splitting leaks test-set information into every filled cell. In a cross-validation loop the imputer belongs inside the fold, next to the scaler.

The decision rule: drop rows only when missingness is tiny and clearly unrelated to the outcome. Use median or mode plus a missingness indicator as the workhorse default. Move to iterative imputation when a column has many gaps, correlates strongly with others, and matters to the model. And when a column is more than half missing, seriously consider dropping the column instead of the rows.

interview.question: Why is mean imputation not a neutral choice?
interview.answer: It asserts that the missing values resemble the average of the observed ones, which only holds if data is missing completely at random. It also creates an artificial spike at one value, shrinking the column's variance and typically weakening its measured relationship with the target. When missingness is driven by the value itself, mean-filling erases precisely the extreme cases you cared about.

interview.question: When is dropping rows with missing values the right call?
interview.answer: When the affected fraction is small enough that the data loss is immaterial and you have reason to believe the missingness is unrelated to the outcome. If either condition fails, you are either throwing away real signal or introducing selection bias into every subsequent estimate. It is also unavailable at prediction time, when you must produce an answer for a row that has a gap.

interview.question: Why add a missingness indicator when you have already imputed the value?
interview.answer: Because the fact of absence often carries information that the filled value cannot express — a declined income question or a failed sensor reading is itself predictive. The indicator lets the model separate that signal from the imputed number, rather than forcing one column to encode both. It costs one binary column and frequently improves results more than a more sophisticated imputer would.

feature-selection-methods.text: More columns is not more information. Features that carry no signal still contribute noise the model can fit, features that duplicate each other make coefficients unstable, and every extra column costs compute and makes the result harder to explain. Selection picks a subset of the original columns and discards the rest. Filter methods score each feature independently and keep the top ones. Wrapper methods repeatedly train the model on candidate subsets and keep whichever wins. Embedded methods let the model itself zero out features during fitting. The three differ mainly in cost and fidelity.
feature-selection-methods.deep_text:
Say you have 500 columns and 3,000 rows. A filter approach computes something like the correlation between each column and the target, or a mutual information score, and keeps the top 50. It costs one pass over the data and is trivially parallel. What it misses is interaction: a column that is useless alone but highly predictive in combination with another scores near zero and gets dropped. Filters are also blind to redundancy, so ten near-identical columns can all score highly and all survive.

Wrapper methods evaluate subsets by actually training. Recursive feature elimination is the common version: fit the model on all 500 columns, rank features by the model's own importance measure, drop the weakest handful, refit, and repeat until you hit a target count. That is dozens of model fits, and every one of them must be scored on held-out data or you will simply select whatever fits the training noise best. Wrappers respect the model's actual behaviour, including interactions, which is why they usually outperform filters when you can afford them.

Embedded methods get selection for free during fitting. An L1 penalty added to a linear model's loss drives coefficients of unhelpful features exactly to zero, so the fitted model hands you a subset directly. Tree ensembles produce importance scores as a by-product of splitting. One fit, and you have both a model and a ranking.

The common misconception is that selection is fundamentally about speed. Speed is a side effect; the real win is variance reduction. With 500 columns and 3,000 rows, some columns will correlate with the target by chance alone, and a flexible model will latch onto them. Removing them makes the model's estimate more stable across resamples, which is what actually shows up as better held-out performance.

The trap that ruins more experiments than any other: running selection on the full dataset before splitting. If you rank 500 features by correlation with the target computed across all rows, then split and evaluate, your test rows helped choose the features and your score is inflated — sometimes dramatically, when the true signal is weak. Selection belongs inside the cross-validation fold.

The decision rule: use a filter as a cheap first cut when you have thousands of columns and need to get to a manageable number. Use an embedded method as the default working choice, since it costs one fit. Reserve wrappers for a final refinement when the feature count is already modest and the compute budget allows repeated training.

interview.question: Why does removing features sometimes improve held-out accuracy even though you have discarded information?
interview.answer: Because irrelevant features still let the model fit noise, and with limited rows some of them will correlate with the target by chance. The model spends capacity on those spurious relationships, which do not hold on new data. Dropping them reduces the variance of the fitted model, and that variance reduction usually outweighs the tiny amount of genuine signal lost.

interview.question: What goes wrong if you select features before splitting into train and test?
interview.answer: The selection step has seen the test labels, so the surviving features were chosen partly because they happen to work on the test rows. Your test score then measures the selection procedure's luck as well as the model, and it comes out optimistically biased. The correct pattern is to perform selection inside each cross-validation fold, using only that fold's training data.

interview.question: When would you prefer a wrapper method over an embedded one?
interview.answer: When feature interactions matter and the model's built-in importance measure does not reflect them well, and when the candidate set is small enough that repeated refits are affordable. Wrappers evaluate subsets by the metric you actually care about, so they can catch cases an embedded ranking misses. The costs are compute and a higher risk of overfitting the selection itself, so the evaluation must be on held-out folds.

principal-component-analysis.text: When many columns say roughly the same thing, you can replace them with a smaller set of new columns that keep most of the variation. PCA does this by finding the directions in which the data spreads out most, ranking them, and projecting onto the top few. The first component is the single direction of greatest variance, the second is the best remaining direction perpendicular to it, and so on. Unlike keeping a subset of original columns, the outputs are blends of everything, so you gain compactness and lose the ability to name what each new column means.
principal-component-analysis.deep_text:
Picture height in centimetres and weight in kilograms across a population. The two are strongly correlated, so the cloud of points forms a long diagonal ellipse. PCA finds the long axis of that ellipse — a direction roughly like "overall body size" — as the first component, and the short axis perpendicular to it as the second. If the first component captures 95 percent of the variance, you can describe each person with one number instead of two and lose very little. Scale that up: 200 correlated sensor readings might reduce to 15 components that retain 90 percent of the variance, cutting the model's input width by more than an order of magnitude.

Mechanically, you centre the data, compute the covariance matrix, and take its eigenvectors. Each eigenvector is a component direction and its eigenvalue is the variance along that direction. Sorting by eigenvalue gives the ranking. In practice you choose how many components to keep by looking at cumulative explained variance — keep enough to reach 90 or 95 percent — or by finding the point where the curve visibly bends and additional components stop buying much.

Scaling is not optional here. PCA maximises variance, and variance depends on units, so a column measured in metres and one measured in millimetres contribute wildly differently to the same underlying quantity. Run PCA on unstandardised data and the first component will simply point along whichever column has the largest raw numbers. Standardise first unless every column is already in the same units and you deliberately want the raw magnitudes to matter.

The common misconception is that high variance means high predictive value. PCA never looks at the target. A direction with large spread can be pure measurement noise, and a low-variance direction can hold the entire signal you care about. It is entirely possible for the top components to be useless for prediction while a discarded one was the important one, which is why you should always compare against a model on the untransformed features rather than assuming the reduction helped.

The second misconception is that components are interpretable. Each is a weighted combination of every original column, so "component 3" has no natural meaning; you can inspect its loadings and sometimes tell a story, but it is not a feature you can explain to a stakeholder the way a named column can.

The decision rule: reach for PCA when columns are numerous and clearly correlated, when you need to fight the instability that comes from having more columns than rows, or when you want a two-dimensional projection for plotting. Avoid it when interpretability is a requirement, when the relationships are strongly non-linear so that a linear projection misrepresents the structure, or when the feature count is already small enough to handle directly.

interview.question: Why must you standardise features before running PCA?
interview.answer: PCA finds directions of maximum variance, and variance is measured in the units of each column, so a column with large raw numbers dominates regardless of how much information it carries. Without standardisation the first component often just tracks whichever feature has the biggest scale. Standardising puts every column on equal footing so the components reflect correlation structure rather than unit choice.

interview.question: PCA is unsupervised. When does that bite you?
interview.answer: When the predictive signal lives in a low-variance direction. Since PCA ranks directions purely by spread and never consults the target, it can discard exactly the component that mattered while keeping ones that are mostly noise. The safeguard is to treat the component count as a hyperparameter tuned against validation performance, and to always compare with a baseline trained on the untransformed features.

interview.question: When would you use feature selection rather than PCA to reduce dimensionality?
interview.answer: When you need to explain the model, or when downstream consumers act on individual features. Selection keeps original columns that retain their names and meanings, whereas PCA produces blends of everything that nobody can interpret directly. Selection is also preferable when only a handful of columns carry signal and the rest are genuinely irrelevant, since PCA would still mix that noise into every component.

hyperparameter-tuning.text: Some numbers a model uses are learned from data. Others you have to pick before training starts — how strongly to regularise, how deep a tree may grow, how large a step to take. Those choices often matter more than the algorithm itself, and there is no formula for them, so you search. This part starts by drawing the line between what is learned and what is chosen, then works through how to search that space efficiently, and finally how to score candidates honestly enough that the winner is genuinely better rather than luckier.
hyperparameter-tuning.deep_text:
The first part is definitional but load-bearing: until you can say which numbers the fitting procedure sets and which you set yourself, the rest of the topic has no object. It also explains why hyperparameters cannot simply be optimised alongside the parameters — they are chosen on a different criterion, evaluated on different data.

The middle two parts are competing search strategies, and they sit next to each other on purpose. Exhaustive and random sampling of the space are the baseline approaches: simple, embarrassingly parallel, and requiring no assumptions. They are also blind, spending exactly as much effort on hopeless regions as on promising ones. The alternative builds a model of how settings map to performance and uses it to decide where to look next, which costs bookkeeping and sequential dependency but converges in far fewer trials. Understanding the first makes the second's motivation obvious, so the order matters.

The final part is the foundation the other three stand on, placed last because its necessity is clearest once you have seen the search. Every strategy compares candidates by a score, and if that score is noisy or contaminated, the search optimises the noise. A single train-validation split has enough variance that the reported winner is frequently arbitrary, and repeated evaluation against the same split gradually fits the search to it. Resampling strategies control both problems, and knowing which strategy suits which data — imbalanced classes, grouped observations, time-ordered rows — determines whether the whole exercise produced anything real.

The practical thread connecting all four: tuning is an outer loop, and its cost is the number of candidates multiplied by the cost of evaluating one. Every decision here is a trade between those two factors.

parameters-vs-hyperparameters.text: Parameters are the numbers the fitting procedure discovers from your data — the coefficients in a linear model, the split thresholds in a tree, the cluster centres. You never set them by hand; training's whole job is to find them. Hyperparameters are the numbers you fix before training begins, which shape how that search runs or how flexible the resulting model is allowed to be. Learning rate, regularisation strength, number of trees, maximum depth, cluster count. The distinction matters because they are chosen by different means and validated on different data.
parameters-vs-hyperparameters.deep_text:
Take ridge regression on a dataset with 20 features. Fitting produces 20 coefficients plus an intercept — 21 parameters, all determined by minimising the penalised error on the training rows. But the penalty has a strength, usually written as alpha or lambda, and that is a hyperparameter. Set it to 0.01 and you get one set of 21 coefficients; set it to 100 and you get a different, much smaller set. Nothing in the training procedure tells you which alpha to use, because the training objective is monotone in it — a larger penalty always makes training error worse, so minimising training error would always pick alpha equal to zero.

That is the crux. Hyperparameters cannot be chosen by the criterion that chooses parameters, because they usually control the flexibility-versus-fit trade that the training objective is deliberately blind to. Their criterion is held-out performance, which is why tuning requires a separate evaluation set and why the whole apparatus of validation exists.

A random forest makes the same point differently. Its parameters are every split threshold and leaf value across every tree — potentially millions of numbers, none of them typed by a human. Its hyperparameters are a handful: how many trees, how deep, how many features to consider per split, the minimum samples in a leaf. A handful of chosen numbers determines the shape of millions of learned ones.

The common misconception is that hyperparameters are just settings that could in principle be learned if we were cleverer. Some can, in a limited sense — early stopping effectively learns the number of boosting rounds by watching a validation curve. But that only works because it evaluates on data outside the training fit, which is precisely the defining feature of hyperparameter selection rather than an exception to it.

A related confusion is the status of the random seed or the number of CPU cores. Those affect the run but are not hyperparameters in the meaningful sense, because you are not searching over them for better generalisation. Seed sensitivity is a variance problem to measure, not a knob to tune — if changing the seed changes your validation score more than changing the regularisation does, your evaluation is too noisy to draw conclusions from.

The practical rule: any number you had to type before calling fit, which changes the model's behaviour and has no obviously correct value, is a hyperparameter and belongs in your search space. Any number the fit call produced is a parameter and belongs to the model.

interview.question: Why can't hyperparameters be learned by the same optimisation that learns parameters?
interview.answer: Because the training objective is typically monotone in them — a weaker regularisation penalty always lowers training error, so minimising training error would drive the penalty to zero every time. Hyperparameters control the trade between fit and flexibility, and that trade is only visible on data the fit did not see. Their selection criterion is therefore held-out performance, evaluated in an outer loop.

interview.question: Is the random seed a hyperparameter?
interview.answer: Not in any useful sense. It changes the outcome but you are not searching over it to improve generalisation, and picking the seed with the best validation score is just fitting noise. It is better treated as a variance measurement: run several seeds and look at the spread. If that spread is comparable to the differences between your candidate settings, the tuning results are not trustworthy.

interview.question: Where does early stopping fit in this distinction?
interview.answer: It selects a hyperparameter — the number of iterations or boosting rounds — but does so automatically by monitoring a validation curve during training. That is consistent with the definition rather than an exception, because the decision is made on data the fit is not using. The important consequence is that the early-stopping set is spent and cannot double as your final evaluation set.

grid-search-and-random-search.text: The simplest way to tune is to try things. Grid search enumerates every combination of the values you listed for each hyperparameter, trains a model for each, and keeps the best. Random search instead samples combinations from ranges you specify, running a fixed budget of trials wherever they land. Both are trivially parallel and require no assumptions about how the parameters interact. The surprising result is that for the same number of trials, random usually beats grid — because most hyperparameters barely matter, and grid wastes its budget re-testing them.
grid-search-and-random-search.deep_text:
Make the comparison concrete. You want to tune learning rate and maximum tree depth. A grid with five learning rates and four depths is 20 combinations, and with 5-fold cross-validation that is 100 model fits. Every one of those five learning rates is tested at exactly four distinct values — you learn about five points along the learning rate axis, no more, no matter how many depths you add.

Now run random search with the same 20 trials, sampling learning rate log-uniformly and depth uniformly. Each trial draws a fresh learning rate, so you cover 20 distinct values along that axis instead of five. If learning rate is the parameter that actually matters and depth barely moves the score — which is the usual situation — random search has explored the important dimension four times as finely for identical cost. Add a third hyperparameter and grid's cost multiplies while random's stays fixed at 20; that multiplication is what makes exhaustive search collapse beyond three or four dimensions.

The common misconception is that grid search is more thorough. It is exhaustive only over the points you happened to list, and those points are usually a coarse guess. A grid of 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 for learning rate will never find that 0.03 was the right answer, whereas continuous sampling can land near it. Thoroughness over an arbitrary lattice is not thoroughness over the space.

Getting the sampling distribution right matters as much as the choice of method. Learning rate and regularisation strength should be sampled on a log scale, because their effect is multiplicative — uniform sampling between 0.0001 and 1 puts 90 percent of the draws above 0.1 and effectively never tests the small end. Integer parameters like tree depth or neighbour count sample fine uniformly.

Both methods share one hazard: with enough trials, the best validation score is partly luck. If you run 200 trials and pick the winner by validation score, that score is optimistically biased, because you selected the maximum of 200 noisy numbers. Report final performance on a test set the search never touched.

The decision rule: use grid when the space is small, discrete, and you genuinely want every combination — two or three parameters with a few levels each, or a final refinement in a narrow region you have already localised. Use random for everything else, especially initial exploration and any space with more than three dimensions. Both are the right call when trials are cheap and parallel; when each trial takes hours, a smarter sequential method earns its complexity.

interview.question: Why does random search typically outperform grid search at the same budget?
interview.answer: Because hyperparameters differ enormously in importance, and grid search tests only as many distinct values per parameter as you listed, regardless of budget. Random search draws a new value on every axis each trial, so it explores the parameters that matter far more finely for the same cost. Grid also multiplies combinatorially with each added dimension, while random's cost is whatever budget you set.

interview.question: How would you set the sampling distribution for a regularisation strength?
interview.answer: Log-uniform over several orders of magnitude, because the effect is multiplicative — the difference between 0.001 and 0.01 is large while 0.5 and 0.51 are indistinguishable. Uniform sampling would concentrate nearly all draws in the top decade and effectively never test small values. The same reasoning applies to learning rate; integer-valued parameters like depth are fine uniform.

interview.question: You ran 300 trials and your best validation score is 0.91. What do you report?
interview.answer: Not 0.91. Taking the maximum over 300 noisy estimates is itself a selection process, so that number is optimistically biased even though every individual estimate was unbiased. I would refit the winning configuration and evaluate once on a test set that took no part in the search, and report that figure as the honest estimate.

bayesian-optimisation.text: Blind search wastes trials on regions it has already learned are bad. Bayesian optimisation fixes that by building a probabilistic model of how hyperparameter settings map to validation score, using every result so far. That surrogate model predicts both an expected score and an uncertainty for any untried setting, and an acquisition function combines the two to choose where to look next — balancing exploiting the region that looks best against exploring where it knows least. It typically finds good settings in far fewer trials, which matters when a single trial costs hours.
bayesian-optimisation.deep_text:
Walk through the loop. You run five random configurations first, to have something to fit. Say learning rates of 0.3, 0.001, 0.05, 0.2, and 0.01 gave validation scores of 0.71, 0.74, 0.86, 0.79, and 0.82. A surrogate — commonly a Gaussian process, or a tree-based estimator when the space has categorical and conditional structure — fits a curve through those points with confidence bands that pinch tight near observed values and flare wide in the gaps. Around 0.05 the predicted score is high and the uncertainty is low. Around 0.1 there is no observation at all, so the uncertainty is wide, and the upper edge of that band might exceed 0.86.

The acquisition function turns that into a decision. Expected improvement, the most common choice, scores each candidate by how much it is expected to beat the current best, integrating over the surrogate's uncertainty. A point with a mediocre mean but huge variance can outscore a point with a good mean and no variance, which is exactly the exploration behaviour you want. You evaluate the winner, add it to the observations, refit the surrogate, and repeat. Over 30 trials the model concentrates its sampling where the score is genuinely high.

Compare that to a blind method needing perhaps 200 trials for a comparable result. If one trial is thirty seconds, nobody cares. If one trial is four hours on a rented machine, the difference is a day versus a fortnight, and the surrogate's overhead is negligible against it.

The common misconception is that Bayesian optimisation is strictly better and should be the default. It is sequential by construction — each trial depends on the previous results — so it parallelises poorly, and 200 blind trials running simultaneously across a cluster can finish sooner in wall-clock time than 30 sequential smart ones. It also carries its own settings, and on a small or noisy space the surrogate can misfit and confidently steer you into a poor region.

A second misconception is that it is immune to the selection bias that afflicts any search: it is not. It is arguably worse, since it actively pursues the maximum of a noisy objective, so its reported best score is optimistic and needs a clean held-out evaluation just the same.

The decision rule: reach for it when each trial is expensive — hours of compute, or a real cost per evaluation — and your budget is measured in tens rather than hundreds of trials, and you have limited parallelism. Stick with blind sampling when trials are cheap, the cluster is wide, or the search space is small enough that the surrogate has nothing to learn.

interview.question: What does the acquisition function actually do?
interview.answer: It converts the surrogate's prediction into a single number scoring how worthwhile each untried configuration is, and the search evaluates whichever scores highest. It has to weigh the predicted score against the uncertainty, so a setting with a mediocre mean but wide confidence bands can be worth trying over a safe known-good one. That balance is what stops the search from collapsing onto the first decent region it finds.

interview.question: When would you deliberately choose random search over Bayesian optimisation?
interview.answer: When trials are cheap and I have wide parallelism. Bayesian optimisation is inherently sequential, since each proposal depends on prior results, so a few hundred random trials fired across a cluster can finish in less wall-clock time than a few dozen sequential informed ones. I would also avoid it on very small or very noisy search spaces, where the surrogate has little to learn and can misfit confidently.

interview.question: Does Bayesian optimisation reduce the risk of overfitting the validation set?
interview.answer: No, it tends to increase it. It deliberately hunts for the maximum of a noisy objective, so it is more likely than blind sampling to find a configuration that scored well by luck on your particular folds. The mitigations are the usual ones: use repeated or nested cross-validation for the search score, and confirm the winner on a test set that the search never saw.

cross-validation-strategies.text: A single train-validation split gives one number, and that number has real variance — reshuffle and the ranking of your candidate models can flip. Cross-validation reduces that noise by splitting the data several ways, training and scoring on each, and averaging. K-fold is the standard: divide into k parts, hold each out in turn. But the right splitting scheme depends on your data. Imbalanced classes need stratification, repeated measurements on the same subject need grouping, and time-ordered data must never train on the future.
cross-validation-strategies.deep_text:
Concretely, 5-fold cross-validation on 10,000 rows means five models: each trains on 8,000 rows and scores on the 2,000 it did not see, and you average the five scores. If those five come out as 0.82, 0.79, 0.85, 0.81, and 0.83, the mean is 0.82 and the spread of roughly 0.03 tells you how much confidence to place in it. That spread is the number people ignore and shouldn't: if two candidate configurations differ by 0.01 while the fold-to-fold spread is 0.03, you have not shown one is better.

Stratification matters when classes are imbalanced. With 3 percent positives, a plain random 5-fold split can produce a fold with 1 percent positives and another with 6 percent purely by chance, so scores swing for reasons unrelated to the model. Stratified splitting preserves the class proportion in every fold and removes that source of variance for free.

Grouping matters when rows are not independent. If you have 200 patients with 10 measurements each, a random split puts the same patient in both train and validation, and the model can recognise that individual rather than learn the underlying pattern. Your score then measures memorisation of specific patients and collapses on new ones. Group-aware splitting keeps all of a patient's rows on one side of every split.

Time ordering is the strictest constraint. Standard k-fold trains on rows that occurred after the validation rows, which is impossible at prediction time and inflates the score, sometimes enormously. Forward-chaining is the fix: train on the first three months and validate on the fourth, then train on four and validate on the fifth, and so on. It gives fewer folds and less training data in the early ones, and that is the honest cost.

The common misconception is that more folds is always better. Leave-one-out cross-validation, where k equals the number of rows, gives an almost unbiased estimate but a high-variance one, because the training sets across folds are nearly identical and the individual scores are perfectly correlated errors on single rows. It also costs one fit per row. Five or ten folds is the usual sweet spot between bias, variance, and compute.

The second and more consequential point: when cross-validation is used to select hyperparameters, the resulting best score is not an unbiased estimate of future performance, because the selection consumed the folds. Nested cross-validation — an inner loop for tuning, an outer loop purely for estimation — is the rigorous fix, at the cost of multiplying the fits. A single clean held-out test set is the cheap approximation most teams actually use.

The decision rule: default to stratified k-fold with 5 or 10 folds. Switch to group-aware splitting the moment rows share an entity, and to forward-chaining the moment prediction happens forward in time. Never do both a search and a final estimate on the same folds.

interview.question: Why is standard k-fold wrong for time series data?
interview.answer: Because folds are assigned randomly, so most training sets contain rows from after the validation period. The model gets to see the future while predicting the past, which is impossible in deployment, and the resulting score is inflated — often dramatically when the series is autocorrelated. Forward-chaining, where each fold trains only on data preceding its validation window, is the correct scheme.

interview.question: You have multiple rows per customer. What splitting scheme do you use and why?
interview.answer: Group-aware splitting keyed on customer, so every row for a given customer lands entirely in train or entirely in validation. A random split lets the model recognise individual customers from their other rows, which is memorisation that will not transfer to new customers. The grouped score is lower, but it is the number that reflects what happens in production.

interview.question: You used 5-fold cross-validation to pick hyperparameters and your best mean score was 0.88. Is that your expected production performance?
interview.answer: No — those folds were consumed by the selection, so 0.88 is the maximum over many noisy estimates and is biased upward. The rigorous answer is nested cross-validation, with an inner loop doing the tuning and an outer loop producing the estimate. In practice most teams hold out a test set that the search never touched and report that instead.
